series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/1] mm, swap: only prefer nonfull clusters on synchronous devices
series_items.patch_summary: The patch partially reverts a previous change that preferred non-full clusters over free ones for all devices, except synchronous devices like zram. It introduces a new function `swap_prefer_free_cluster` to determine whether to prefer free clusters based on the device's flags. This is done to improve write performance by keeping swapout batches contiguous and allowing writes to be merged.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with zswap and suggested adding a best-effort check for zswappability. The patch author's approach to preferring non-full clusters on synchronous devices is generally accepted, but the reviewer wonders if it should also be applied to zswap.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 5, 2026 at 8:51 AM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:
>
> Commit 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters") made
> allocations fill the nonfull clusters of their order before taking a
> free one, on every device without discard. Since commit 3cedb745d354
> ("mm: clarify the folio_free_swap() for do_swap_page()"), an exclusive
> write fault frees the swap slot, so a workload that rewrites swapped out
> memory leaves holes in full clusters, which then go back on the nonfull
> list. Reclaim allocates slots one folio at a time, so a batch of folios
> gets scattered over those holes, its writes can't be merged and it is
> written with many small requests.
>
> So partially revert commit 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over
> free clusters") and prefer free clusters again, except on synchronous
> devices like zram: they don't merge I/O, so the contiguity of the slots
> doesn't matter to them, and filling the holes first keeps the free
> clusters for large folios.
>
> Fixes: 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters")
> Suggested-by: Kairui Song <kasong@tencent.com>
> Signed-off-by: Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr>

LGTM for the most part:

Reviewed-by: Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com>

Quick comment below:

> ---
>  mm/swapfile.c | 19 +++++++++++++------
>  1 file changed, 13 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)
>
> diff --git a/mm/swapfile.c b/mm/swapfile.c
> index 189f04d8838f..1c1b5d0b724a 100644
> --- a/mm/swapfile.c
> +++ b/mm/swapfile.c
> @@ -973,6 +973,17 @@ static bool __swap_cluster_alloc_entries(struct swap_info_struct *si,
>         return true;
>  }
>
> +/*
> + * Prefer a new cluster over a nonfull one if the device needs discard, to
> + * spread out the writes, or if it is not synchronous, to keep the slots
> + * of a swapout batch contiguous so that its writes can be merged.
> + */
> +static bool swap_prefer_free_cluster(struct swap_info_struct *si)
> +{
> +       return (si->flags & SWP_PAGE_DISCARD) ||
> +              !(si->flags & SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO);
> +}

Side note - I wonder if it's worth it to also prefer non-full clusters
for zswap as well?

It's a bit tricky, but I suppose you can do a best-effort check of the
folio's cgroup's zswappability?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch series addresses a performance regression in Linux kernel version 7.3, which increased swap I/O requests by up to 59% on certain devices. The issue arises from the interaction between two commits: one that prefers non-full clusters over free ones and another that frees swap slots on exclusive write faults. The patch series proposes to only prefer non-full clusters on synchronous devices like zram, where filling holes first keeps free clusters available for large folios.

I believe idea behind include/linux/compiler_attributes.h is to make
attribute wrappers as simple and transparent to use as native compiler
attributes. In particular, this means they should be available in every
kernel compilation unit without any additional effort.

series_items.patch_summary: The patch series aims to improve the page allocation mechanism in the Linux kernel by resetting the can_retry_reserves flag when the slowpath restarts after a cpuset update or zonelist rebuild. series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/12] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the Linux kernel's memory management by detecting and handling zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add operations. The first patch in the series addresses a specific issue where concurrent allocation failures can occur due to spurious allocation failures caused by zonelist rewrites during node onlining.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch without raising any concerns or objections.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
> presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.
>
> However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
> onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
> in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
> allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.
>
> For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
> rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:
>
>   [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
>
> A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
> intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
> CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
> allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.
>
> Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
> configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 08/12] mm/page_alloc: retry allocations that raced with a zonelist rebuild
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where GFP_KERNEL allocations can land in the wrong zone due to concurrent zonelist rebuilds. It introduces a new function, `check_retry_zonelist`, which checks if the zonelist has changed since the allocation was made and retries the allocation if necessary. This is done by freeing the allocated page and retrying the allocation. The patch also adds a new function, `zonelist_iter_sample`, which samples the zonelist sequence number without waiting for the writer to finish. This allows for faster allocation paths to detect concurrent rebuilds and retry allocations accordingly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 09/12] mm/hugetlb: retry the pool walk when the zonelist is rebuilt
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where a hugetlb fault bound to one node can take a pool page from another due to the way the zonelist is rebuilt during zone onlining. The patch introduces checks for zonelist updates and retries the pool walk if the zonelist has changed, ensuring that pages are taken from the correct node. This change fixes an issue where kprobes holding the walk across the online could cause a fault to take a page from the wrong node.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 10/12] mm/page_alloc: retry alloc_contig_pages() when the zonelist is rebuilt

Specifically, it introduces a retry mechanism when the zonelist is rebuilt during zone online operations. This change aims to prevent gigantic hugetlb pages from being allocated in ZONE_MOVABLE and ensures that the correct zone is used for page allocation.

The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.

However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.

For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:

  [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]

A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.

Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

From: Josef Bacik <josef@toxicpanda.com>

When the last memory of a zone goes offline, zone_pcp_reset() frees
zone->per_cpu_pageset and zone->per_cpu_zonestats. Nothing waits for those
who found the zone populated and still use the two pointers. They take
neither the memory hotplug lock nor any other lock which offline_pages()
holds, and some of them can sleep:

  CPU0 vmstat_update()                CPU1 offline_pages()
  refresh_cpu_vm_stats()
    for_each_populated_zone(zone)
      pcp = zone->per_cpu_pageset
      cond_resched()
                                      adjust_present_page_count()
                                      zone_pcp_reset(zone)
                                        free_percpu(zone->per_cpu_pageset)
      decay_pcp_high(zone, pcp)
      __this_cpu_write(pcp->expire, 0)

zone_pcp_update(), show_free_areas() and the readers and writers of the
zonestats. If the per-cpu memory has got a new owner in the meantime, it
is corrupted.

leak them when the zone gets memory again. Keep them instead and let
setup_zone_pageset() and zone_pcp_init() use them again, like it is done
with pgdat->per_cpu_nodestats. Their lists are empty, and their limits
have been calculated for a zone without memory by the
init_per_zone_wmark_min() of offline_pages(), which is what
setup_zone_pageset() would come up with as well.

Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.

load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.

it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
that single load.

Onlining the first block of a zone rebuilds every zonelist in place,
shifting the slots after the new zone.  The iterator approves a slot,
then the allocator loads the zone from it, so a GFP_KERNEL request can
land in ZONE_MOVABLE and a nodemask request on a node outside its mask:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  prepare_alloc_pages()
    first_zones_zonelist(nodemask {1})
      slot 0 (NORMAL1) approved
                                    online_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [NORMAL1, NORMAL2, ...]
                                        -> [MOVABLE1, NORMAL1, ...]
  get_page_from_freelist()
    zone = zonelist_zone(slot 0)    /* MOVABLE1 */
    allocates from MOVABLE1

zonelist_update_seq detects the rebuild, but only the slowpath's failure
exits check it.

Check it whenever an allocation succeeds too, and if it changed, free
the page and retry, as the memcg charge failure path does.  Eligible
pages are dropped as well: zonelists only change when memory comes or
goes, and a retry is simpler than rechecking the page.

Freeing the page does not undo a block the allocation claimed.  A
GFP_KERNEL request that lands in a fresh ZONE_MOVABLE converts a free
block to MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE, which stays until the zone's movable free
list runs out and a movable allocation takes it back.

The fast and bulk paths read the seqlock's raw seqcount without waiting:
an ALLOC_NOLOCK caller can be an NMI that interrupted the writer, and on
PREEMPT_RT the seqlock accessor takes the spinlock.  A sample taken
mid-write costs a retry, or NULL under ALLOC_NOLOCK.
check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 when compiled out, so a backport
without the hot-add change stays harmless.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance regression caused by outdated automatic interleave weights in the Linux kernel's memory policy module (mm/mempolicy). When nodes gain or lose memory, their weights are not recalculated from their reported bandwidths, leading to an uneven distribution of data and potential overload. The patch introduces a new function, wi_state_refresh(), which recomputes the weights based on the recorded bandwidth whenever a node gains or loses its first/last memory. If allocating new weights fails, it warns once and continues with the next recompute starting from the full bandwidth table.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME in btrfs_write_check()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the btrfs_write_check function to honor the FMODE_NOCMTIME flag, which prevents updating the inode's c/mtime when writing files over NFSv4.2. This is necessary because nfsd sets this flag on files with delegated timestamps, and skipping the update ensures that the server's c/mtime does not become newer than the time reported by the delegation holder. The patch fixes a stat-dirty file issue found in git test t1092.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME when punching holes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where Btrfs was updating the c/mtime of files even when FMODE_NOCMTIME was set, which can cause problems for NFS clients holding delegated timestamps. The patch introduces a new function btrfs_should_update_cmtime() to determine whether c/mtime should be updated based on file mode and flags. It then uses this function in btrfs_write_check() and replaces the update_times flag with an argument in btrfs_replace_file_extents(). Finally, it updates btrfs_punch_hole() to skip c/mtime updates for FMODE_NOCMTIME files. This patch fixes a regression introduced by a previous commit that froze c/mtime updates during WRITE_ATTRS delegation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME in fallocate
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Btrfs file system where fallocate operations would update the inode's ctime and mtime even when FMODE_NOCMTIME is set, which prevents such updates. The patch introduces an 'update_times' flag that is passed from btrfs_fallocate() to its helpers, ensuring that these times are only updated when necessary. Additionally, it increments the inode's i_version unconditionally in btrfs_fallocate_update_isize(), as this operation can change the NFS change attribute even if the size extension stays within existing preallocation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME when cloning
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Btrfs file system where cloned files would always update their creation and modification times, even when FMODE_NOCMTIME was set. This is problematic because it allows a client to advance the server's ctime during a CLONE operation, which can cause issues with delegated timestamps. The patch makes btrfs_clone_files() respect FMODE_NOCMTIME by passing no_time_update for destinations that have this flag set. Additionally, it exposes the btrfs_should_update_cmtime() function to reflink.c so that it can be used in other contexts.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes issues in the Btrfs file system where it did not properly handle the FMODE_NOCMTIME flag, which is used to prevent modification of timestamps. The patches correct this behavior in several places, including btrfs_write_check(), punching holes, fallocate, and cloning operations. This fix was tested with the git regression testsuite and is intended for inclusion in Linux kernel version 7.5.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 1/3] mm: zswap: fix shrinker count for the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the zswap shrinker, which incorrectly scales the number of freeable entries on the root memcg's LRU by its compression ratio. The issue arises because the root memcg's stats don't account for its own entries, leading to incorrect scaling and potential data loss. To fix this, the patch uses the zswap pool-wide counters for the root memcg instead, ensuring that all entries are properly accounted for.

review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Nov 2, 2026 at 2:51 PM Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> zswap_shrinker_count() scales the number of freeable entries on a
> memcg's zswap LRU by the memcg's compression ratio. That compression
> ratio is computed from the memcg's MEMCG_ZSWAP_B and MEMCG_ZSWAPPED
> stats.
>

>

> instead. The zswap pool-wide counters cover every zswap entry, including
> those owned by the root memcg.
>
> This also gets rid of having to flush the root memcg's stats, which
> flushes every cgroup in the system.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 2/3] mm: memcg: read root lruvec LRU stats from the node counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the accuracy of LRU (Least Recently Used) statistics in the Linux kernel's memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem by reading the root lruvec LRU stats from the node counters instead of relying on potentially stale rstat flushes. This change is particularly important for global reclaim and refault detection, where accurate statistics are crucial. The patch introduces two new functions, `lruvec_lru_page_state` and its monotonic variant, which read the node counters for the root memcg. This approach eliminates the latency introduced by rstat flushes, reducing the time taken to perform root reclaim from approximately 0.9ms to near-zero. The change also improves the accuracy of LRU statistics, ensuring that they reflect the current state of memory allocation and deallocation in the system.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Yosry Ahmed suggested that the patch could be simplified by directly using the node counters in lruvec_page_state() and lruvec_page_state_monotonic(), as these functions already fallback to node stats when memcg is disabled. They asked if there are cases where the node stats would not be suitable.
review_comments.raw_body:
Why not do this directly in lruvec_page_state() and
lruvec_page_state_monotonic()? They already fallback to node stats if
memcg is disabled, why not do the same for the root? Are there cases
where the node stats are not the right thing to do?

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that there are cases where node counters and root memcg stats may not be equal, specifically citing slab's NR_SLAB_RECLAIMABLE_B and NR_SLAB_UNRECLAIMABLE_B statistics, and explained that this is due to the way slab pages are accounted for in the node counter but only updated in the memcg stats under certain conditions.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Yosry,

Thanks for taking a look at this series! I don't think we're able to
do this directly in lruvec_page_state()/lruvec_page_state_monotonic()
because I think there's still some places where the node stat and the
root memcg stat are not guaranteed to be equal.

The stat I was looking at last week was slab's NR_SLAB_RECLAIMABLE_B
and NR_SLAB_UNRECLAIMABLE_B where for those, the node counter value
can contain memory/stats that wasn't actually charged to any memcg,
which I think means for these cases, the node counter values can be
larger than what reading the root memcg rstat value would give. The
functions I was looking at were account_slab() and
memcg_slab_post_alloc_hook() where the logic adds every new slab page
to the node counter but the memcg stats only get updated if specific
criteria are met (eg the cache had SLAB_ACCOUNT set or the allocation
had the __GFP_ACCOUNT gfp flag set and the allocation was not from a
root memcg).

Thanks,
Joanne

couple, I think. I asked a LLM and it says NR_KERNEL_STACK_KB,
NR_PAGETABLE, NR_SECONDARY_PAGETABLE, NR_VMALLOC, NR_HUGETLB,
WORKINGSET_NODERECLAIM would also need to be excluded. We could add
this special casing in, but we would need to make sure any new stat
that gets added in the future that belongs on the exclusion list gets
put on it. If it's missed, the failure would be silent whereas with a

review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed questioned the distinction made in the patch between 'root memcg stats' and 'node stat', wondering if it's intentional for all statistics, specifically pointing out that memory.stat draws a similar distinction.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed questioned whether the distinction between root memcg stats and node stats is intentional, suggesting that the default behavior should be to have them as the same, and proposed an explicit opt-out approach.
review_comments.raw_body:
Interesting. So for all these stats, root memcg stats (from
memory.stat) is not the same as the node stat? They all draw a
distinction between "accounted to root" vs "not accounted"? I wonder
if this is intentional for all of them.

---

I think we probably want to first understand if these stats are
supposed to be different between the root memcg stats and the node
stats first. Personally, I think the default should be the majority
behavior, which I think is that node stats and root memcg stats are
the same, so I am leaning toward explicit opt-out. Let's also see what
memcg folks think.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author Joanne Koong addressed a concern about how kernel memory allocations are accounted for in the root cgroup, explaining that some allocations (category b) should be linked to the root memcg and others (category a) shouldn't be. She wondered if the original commit's decision to not track kernel memory pages to a given memcg was due to avoiding extra overhead costs.

Author agrees that the suggestion is reasonable and asks for input from other memcg developers.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think there's 2 categories:
a) the allocation isn't acccounted to any memcg (eg kernel page
tables, hugetlb when hugetlb accounting is off, unaccounted slab
caches and kmallocs w/out __GFP_ACCOUNT, and most vmalloc). These
values only get added to the node counter

b) the allocation is accounted, but it comes from a task running in
the root cgroup (eg kernel stacks, user + secondary page tables,
accounted slab, etc)

I think a) has to stay as is since it's not linked to any memcg. For
b), it seems intentional from the original commit that added kernel
memory accounting logic (commit 7ae1e1d0f8ac ("memcg: kmem controller
infrastructure")). The commit message for that explicitly says
tracking kernel memory pages to a given memcg "will happen whenever
the caller includes the flag __GFP_KMEMCG flag and the task belongs to
a memcg other than the root". (__GFP_KMEMCG later became
__GFP_ACCOUNT). I wonder though if this was to avoid extra overhead
costs (eg for systems that don't use cgroups) on the hot paths, since
it would need to do non-trivial per-object work. If root read the node
counters for the stats that are in category b (excluding the stats
that are in both category a and b) instead of going through rstat
(which is what this series does for the LRU stats), there wouldn't
need to be any extra overhead at allocation time, since nothing would
need to be tracked.

---

That seems reasonable to me. memcg folks, do you have any thoughts on this?

Thanks,
Joanne

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch moves the updates of LRU size statistics out of the lru_lock critical section in folio batches, which reduces contention and improves throughput. The stats are accumulated while holding the lock and applied after dropping it, reducing the overhead of cache misses and improving performance. This change is particularly beneficial for workloads with many threads faulting and freeing memory in a single memcg, where the hold time of lru_lock directly limits throughput. The patch also moves cost_lock into the hole after lru_lock to make room for the batch pointer, keeping struct lruvec from growing. The stats may lag behind the LRU lists by one batch, but this is within the per-cpu batching already present.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/5] iomap: remove ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end() legacy path
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the legacy ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end() path in the iomap code, as all in-tree filesystems have implemented the ->iomap_next() method. The changes involve updating the iomap_iter function to use the ->iomap_next() method instead of the legacy path and removing the corresponding flags and functions from the iomap_ops structure. This change simplifies the iomap code and reduces its complexity.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/5] iomap: pass iomap_iter_next_fn directly instead of struct iomap_ops
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the iomap code by removing the struct iomap_ops, which only contained a single function pointer. Instead, the iomap_iter_next_fn is passed directly to the iomap_iter and other entry points. This change is possible because all filesystems now implement ->iomap_next() and have removed the legacy fallback. The patch also renames the ops field in the iomap_iter tracepoint to next for consistency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/5] Documentation: iomap: update docs to reflect iomap_iter_next model
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the iomap documentation to reflect a change in how filesystems interact with the iomap API. Specifically, it removes support for separate ->iomap_begin() and ->iomap_end() callbacks, replacing them with a single iomap_iter_next() callback that finishes the previous mapping (if any) and produces the next one. The patch updates documentation across three files to reflect this change.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series converts various filesystems to use the new iomap_iter_next model, which replaces the legacy ->iomap_begin() and ->iomap_end() functions. The patches are rebased on current mainline and include preparatory patches for nilfs2 and fuse iomap code. The changes also update documentation to reflect the new model. The series applies cleanly to both current mainline and next-20261027, but conflicts may arise by the time it is picked up at the end of the merge window.

Re: [PATCH v2] mm: move LRU size stat updates out of lru_lock in folio batches
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Joanne Koong posted a v3 of the patch addressing David Hildenbrand's suggestion to add documentation about a potential race condition between reparenting and stats updates.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong
review_comments.summary: Posted a v3 addressing David Hildenbrand's suggestion to add documentation about a potential race condition between reparenting and stats updates.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 5, 2026 at 11:53 AM Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thu, Nov 5, 2026 at 11:37 AM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
> <david@kernel.org> wrote:
> >
> > On 10/30/26 01:19, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> > > On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 01:41:57PM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
> > >> folio_batch_move_lru() and folios_put_refs() take the lruvec's lru_lock
> > >> once per batch, but they update the node and memcg lruvec stats for
> > >> every folio in the batch while holding the lock. Only the LRU lists and
> > >> the memcg lru_zone_size need lru_lock. Updating the stats while holding
> > >> the lru_lock is unnecessary, and they make up a large part of the
> > >> critical section, as seen in [1] where a change that added just a few
> > >> instructions to the memcg stat update path cost about 2% throughput
> > >> because the LRU stat updates run under lru_lock, and the overhead went
> > >> away once they were moved outside of the lock.
> > >>
> > >> With many threads faulting and freeing memory in a single memcg, about
> > >> half of all cycles are spent waiting for lru_lock, and the hold time of
> > >> the lru_lock directly limits throughput. A perf profile with 80 threads
> > >> faulting in and freeing shmem in a single memcg shows 52.8% of all
> > >> cycles spent spinning on lru_lock, split evenly between
> > >> folio_batch_move_lru() and folios_put_refs(). About 25% of the time
> > >> spent holding lru_lock in those two paths goes to the LRU stat updates,
> > >> mostly cache misses loading pn->memcg, pn->lruvec_stats_percpu and the
> > >> per-cpu counters. The stat updates are only 0.7% of all cycles, but they
> > >> lengthen the critical section that the other threads are waiting on.
> > >>
> > >> Accumulate the stat changes per LRU list while holding the lock instead,
> > >> and only apply them after dropping the lock (while still inside
> > >> the RCU read section that keeps the lruvec's memcg alive). This moves
> > >> the stat updates out of the lru_lock critical section and turns the
> > >> per-folio updates into at most one update per LRU list per batch.
> > >
> > > This updating of stats after dropping the lru lock does introduce one behavior
> > > change i.e. race between reparenting on offlining and stats update. I think it
> > > is safe and correct though. Better to document it.
> > >
> > >>
> > >> The batch is attached to the lruvec while lru_lock is held so that the
> > >> LRU add/del helpers don't need to pass it down. To keep struct lruvec
> > >> from growing, cost_lock is moved into the hole after lru_lock, which
> > >> leaves room for the batch pointer in the same cacheline as lru_lock.
> > >>
> > >> The stats can now lag behind the LRU lists by one batch, which is well
> > >> within the per-cpu batching they already have.
> > >>
> > >> On a 2-socket Skylake (80 CPUs, 2 NUMA nodes), with threads pinned to
> > >> CPUs repeatedly faulting in and freeing memory in a single memcg,
> > >> average pages per second over 7 freshly created memcgs per run, 2 boots
> > >> each:
> > >>
> > >>                      before    after
> > >>   shmem, 20 threads  4.74M     5.47M   (+15%)
> > >>   shmem, 80 threads  7.94M    10.33M   (+30%)
> > >>   anon,  20 threads  3.04M     3.35M   (+10%)
> > >>   anon,  80 threads  3.23M     3.41M   (+5%)
> > >>
> > >> Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-fsdevel/CAJnrk1ZezmmzrYdf8KP6re_a76izMS=qGPeC8ZZXiteHyZZC-Q@mail.gmail.com/ [1]
> > >> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
> > >
> > > Acked-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>
> > >
> >
> > Thanks, I'm planning on queue this.
> >
>
> I'll send out a v3 today that adds the documentation Shakeel suggested
> about the race between reparenting on offlining and stats update.
>

I'm seeing that the patch was picked up yesterday into mm-new. Could
you or Andrew add this paragraph to the commit message after the
"Accumulate the stats changes..." paragraph?:

"Applying the stats after dropping lru_lock means a batched update can
race with reparenting when the memcg is being offlined. This is ok
because updates to a dying memcg are redirected to its nearest
non-dying ancestor, which is where its folios end up after
reparenting."

Apologies for any inconveniences.

Thanks,
Joanne
